units: an acquaintance of the narrator records her inner states in a notebook
she writes down the moral exhaustion that arrives at the end of the week with no clear cause
she spots her irritation in the way she slams the cupboards shut
she also notes the worry that comes before a dreaded exchange
she marks down feeling relieved, since that state fades from memory too quickly
she records the embarrassment that reddens her cheeks after an unfortunate remark
the narrator asks her what this record is good for
the woman answers that she wants to recognize herself, not reform herself
she claims that naming an inner state by its name already calms it
text: A friend told me the other evening that she keeps a notebook of her moods, and she walked me through what goes into it. Weariness comes first, the kind that drops on her at the end of the week for no reason she can name and leaves her wanting nothing. Then irritation, which she catches in the way she slams the cupboard doors shut. Worry gets a line of its own, the sort that circles the kitchen with her before a conversation she dreads. She writes down relief as well, she said, because that one slips out of memory as soon as the fear lifts. Last comes embarrassment, the prickle in her cheeks after she says something clumsy. I asked her what the whole list was good for. She said she is not trying to correct herself, only to recognize herself, and that putting a name to a feeling usually takes the sting out of it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the way low spirits are accounted for has changed over the generations
the earliest healers put dejection down to an imbalance of the blood
they treated that dejection by drawing blood off
a later stage consisted in shutting the sick away from public view
that confinement was not aimed at curing them
physicians then began gathering and writing down what their patients told them
the houses of care were fitted with gardens, walking paths and workshops
it was assumed at the time that steady occupation settled the mind
conversation became a means of care in its turn
today's listening rooms carry the mark of those successive stages
text: The words people use for low spirits have shifted from one generation to the next, and the shifts fall into stages that can be read in order. The earliest healers filed dark moods under disorders of the blood and drew blood off to correct them. Confinement came next: the afflicted were shut away, not to be cured but to be kept out of common sight. A generation later, physicians began listening to what their patients told them and copying the complaints into ledgers. Houses of care were then given gardens, walking paths and workshops, on the assumption that steady occupation settled a restless mind. Closer to our own time, talk itself turned into a remedy, and listening became a craft that had to be taught. Every one of those stages has left its mark on the rooms where people are heard today.

units: a grievance that repeats and is never spoken leaves a lasting imprint on memory
silence turns into a store where what went unsaid piles up
that pile breeds a stubborn grudge
the grudge makes old memories sharper than they truly were
the person replays the scene in his mind through the night
that chewing burns the energy meant for the people close to him
a quiet withdrawal from company sets in afterwards
the solitude allows no contradiction and so strengthens the grievance
getting out of the circle means saying the thing aloud, clumsily if need be
text: An annoyance that keeps coming back and is never spoken wears a groove into memory. Silence feels comfortable at first, then turns into a storeroom where everything left unsaid gets piled up. Out of that pile grows a stubborn grudge, and the grudge lends old scenes an edge the events themselves never had. At night the sleeper goes back over them, stages the exchange again, supplies the lines that should have been delivered. The chewing wears him down, since the mind spends on an absent opponent the energy the people close to him deserve. Withdrawal follows, quietly: an invitation is turned down, a call is cut short, solitude gets chosen and blamed on tiredness. And because solitude leaves nothing to contradict the grievance, it confirms it instead of putting it out. Getting free means saying the thing aloud, clumsily if need be.

units: a trainer in charge of a night team described this case in a report
the verbal clashes happened mostly at the close of the shift
a look at the data ruled out production load as the main cause
the busiest stretches fell earlier in the shift
the tensions broke out after the second scheduled break
alertness and resistance to frustration both drop at that moment
the handover meeting was moved to the opening of the shift
its length was cut and an order of speaking was imposed
a form on inner state, filled in on arrival and on leaving, served as the indicator
the reported incidents fell after one full cycle
text: A trainer responsible for a night team wrote the following case into an internal report. Verbal incidents clustered at the close of the shift, where operators lost their tempers with one another again and again. A look at the logs ruled out production load as the main driver, since the busiest stretches fell much earlier. What the records did show was that exchanges soured after the second scheduled break, the point where alertness drops and tolerance for frustration goes with it. The protocol adopted moved the handover meeting to the opening of the shift, cut its length, and imposed a fixed order of speaking. A mood form, filled in on arrival and again on leaving, supplied the measure. One full cycle later the reported incidents had fallen, and the team described a calm that held.

units: two calming methods must be told apart before being used against a surge of anxiety
the first method means controlling the breath while seated, one hand on the belly
the breathing out must last longer than the breathing in, and the cycle repeats
this method takes hold very quickly and calls for no equipment
its effect fades as soon as the irritation shows up again
the second method means writing the fear down and setting beside it what makes it unlikely
the page must be read again at the end of the day
this second method asks for more effort and comforts less on the spot
its benefit, on the other hand, holds for several weeks
combining the breath for the emergency and the writing for the underlying trouble is advised
text: Two calming methods deserve to be told apart before either is turned on a rising wave of anxiety. The first works on the breath. Sit down, rest one hand on the belly, draw air in slowly, then let it out over a longer count, and repeat the cycle until the pulse eases. Its strength is speed: it takes hold within moments and calls for no equipment at all. Its weakness is how long the effect holds, because it fades the moment the irritation comes back. The second method works on words. Write down the exact fear, set beside it whatever makes that outcome unlikely, and read the page again at the end of the day. It asks for more effort and gives less comfort on the spot, yet what it gives holds for weeks. In practice, pair them: breath for the emergency, writing for the underlying trouble.

units: a place for people to be heard has been fitted out in a former storage building
its staff set out several uses of the site
the first use is the walk-in welcome, with no appointment and no paperwork
group meetings bring together visitors touched by the same ordeal
those shared ordeals include the death of someone close, a break-up or the loss of a job
a movement workshop lets tension come loose through walking and stretching
a fourth use consists in sending the heaviest cases on to a specialist
the manager reports that attendance has doubled since the opening
half of the visitors come back again
text: A listening center fitted out inside a former storage building has opened to the public, and the staff there set out several distinct uses for it. The first is the walk-in welcome: anyone can push the door open and talk to a trained listener, with no file to fill in and nothing to justify. The second covers the group meetings, which bring together people carrying the same ordeal, the death of someone close, a break-up, or the loss of a job. The third is a movement workshop, where tension is worked loose by walking and stretching rather than by telling a story. The fourth use, a quieter one, is referral: distress too heavy for a short talk gets passed on to a practitioner. The manager says attendance has doubled since the doors opened, and that half of those who come come back.

units: a child goes down in the middle of the room and the noise takes over the home
the fit starts with a rigid back, balled fists and a locked jaw
the first sob cuts the breathing off
an odd hush follows that first sob
the crying then carries on in wave after wave
the slightest clumsy word sets the wave going again
the face turns red and the hair sticks to the temples
the calm arrives with nothing you can point to and the hiccups come further apart
the child ends up slumped against a shoulder, worn out and surprised at the quiet
he then asks for water as if nothing had happened
text: You have seen it happen: a child goes down in the middle of the living room and the noise takes over the whole place. It starts with the back going rigid, the fists balled, the jaw locked. Then comes the first sob, huge, cutting the breath off and leaving an odd hush behind it. After that the crying settles into waves, up and down and up again the second anyone says the wrong thing. The face turns red, the hair sticks to the temples, the hands grab at whatever cloth is near. Then, with nothing you can point to having changed, the swell weakens. The breath breaks into hiccups that come further and further apart. The shoulders drop at last. The child ends up slumped against a shoulder, worn out, warm, half surprised at the quiet, and asks for a glass of water as if none of it had happened.

units: people are now required to keep an even mood at all times
that demand delivers the opposite of what it aims at
a dark inner state reads as a flaw of character
whoever feels one therefore hides it from those around him
by hiding it, he loses the sharing that would have eased it
the loneliness that results adds still more to the load
the inner state sets hard instead of running its course
a shame at failing then comes on top, heavier than the original hurt
this chain explains the growing number of consultations begun too late
the writer judges it cheaper to let sadness be spoken than to treat it afterwards
text: People are now expected to hold an even mood whatever happens, and the demand delivers the opposite of what it sets out to do. A dark feeling reads as a flaw of character, so whoever carries one keeps it hidden from the people around him. Kept hidden, it gets shared with nobody at all, and the one mechanism that might have eased it goes missing. The loneliness that follows adds to a weight already heavy, so the feeling hardens and settles in rather than running its course. Then comes the shame of not coping with it, heavier by far than the hurt it grew out of. That whole chain is why so many people reach a consulting room late, once the trouble has thickened past what ordinary talk can undo. Letting sadness be spoken aloud would cost a great deal less than treating it after seasons of silence.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who runs a bookbinding workshop did not take up the trade out of a liking for the material
she spoke little and went to pieces in front of a counter clerk
she called off appointments out of fear of being looked at
her life had narrowed until it fit inside two streets
an acquaintance offered her to come and sew sections with no obligation to speak
the change came from the work of the hands itself
her voice came loose while her hands were busy
she first served customers in short sentences, then explained her craft
she ended up training an apprentice
she says the fear is still there but no longer decides how her weeks are spent
text: The woman who runs the bookbinding workshop at the back of the courtyard did not take up the trade out of any love of paper. She spoke little, went to pieces at a counter, and called off appointments rather than be looked at. Her life had narrowed until it fit inside two streets. One season an acquaintance offered her a bench and some sections to sew, with no requirement to say a word to anyone. She stitched whole evenings without lifting her head, and that suited her. What changed things was the work of the hands: with them busy, her voice came loose before she noticed. She answered customers in short sentences at first, then explained what she was doing, then trained an apprentice. The fear has not gone, she says, and it still meets her at a stranger, but it no longer decides how her weeks are spent.

units: two instruments for gauging mood are in use in clinical practice
the first instrument is a short questionnaire the patient fills in himself
its items ask about the week just gone
its internal consistency holds up and the form takes little attention to complete
that lightness allows the measure to be repeated
it is hit by a desirability bias that flatters the profile the respondent reports
the second instrument is a structured interview run by a trained professional
its scoring rests on observed signs as much as on what the person says
it stands up better to the bias but costs a great deal of time and depends on the rater's training
the writer recommends the questionnaire for close follow-up and the interview for settling a diagnosis
text: Two instruments for gauging mood are in circulation in clinical practice, and comparing them repays a close look. The first is a short questionnaire the patient fills in alone, its items asking about the week just gone. Internal consistency holds up well, and the form takes so little attention to complete that the measure can be repeated as often as the follow-up requires. Against that, it carries a desirability bias: respondents paint a rosier picture than they live. The second is a structured interview run by a trained clinician, scored on observed signs as much as on what is said aloud. It stands up better to the bias, but the time it eats makes it expensive, and its reliability rests on how well the rater was drilled. For close monitoring, take the questionnaire; for a diagnosis, the interview.
